title: Automate the firewall with the FMC REST API
blurb: Authenticate to the FMC API, read objects, and create one with a small Python script.
scenario: Adding dozens of host objects by hand in FMC is slow and error-prone. Use the **FMC REST API** at **https://fmc.scor.lab** to authenticate, list network objects, and create a host object from Python.
topology: Python script ── HTTPS ── FMC fmc.scor.lab ── manages FTD devices
objectives: Match HTTP methods to CRUD actions and read status codes
Build the request that creates a host object

steps.title: The token flow
steps.learn: FMC uses **token-based authentication**. You POST your credentials (Basic auth) once, and FMC returns an access token and a domain UUID in the **response headers**. Every later call sends the token in the **X-auth-access-token** header.
steps.task: Put the steps of an API session in order.
steps.question: Order from first call to result.
items: Read X-auth-access-token and DOMAIN_UUID from the response headers
Send GET /api/fmc_config/v1/domain/{DOMAIN_UUID}/object/networks with the token header
Parse the JSON items in the response
Refresh the token before it expires (30 minutes) with /auth/refreshtoken

steps.title: Methods and status codes
steps.learn: REST maps CRUD to HTTP methods: **POST** creates, **GET** reads, **PUT** updates (replaces) and **DELETE** removes. Status codes in the 2xx range mean success, 4xx means a problem with your request, and 5xx means a problem on the server.
steps.task: Match each item to its meaning.

steps.title: Build the request
steps.learn: The Python **requests** library sends the call. The body is JSON describing the object, and the headers carry the token and content type.
steps.task:
Fill in the blanks to create host object **web-srv-01** at **172.16.1.10**:

`r = requests.____(f"{base}/api/fmc_config/v1/domain/{uuid}/object/____", headers={"____": token, "Content-Type": "application/json"}, json={"name": "web-srv-01", "type": "Host", "value": "172.16.1.10"}, verify="fmc-ca.pem")`
steps.hint: Creating is a POST. The collection for single addresses is called hosts. The token header is the one FMC returned.

steps.title: Certificate checking
steps.question: A colleague's script uses `verify=False` to get past a certificate error. Why is that a problem?

options.text: It turns off TLS server verification, so a man in the middle could impersonate FMC and capture the admin credentials and token.

options.why: Speed isn't the issue. Skipping verification removes the protection against impersonation.
verify controls whether the client checks the server, not the other way around.

summary: The FMC token flow, HTTP methods and status codes, a Python POST that creates a host object with the access token header, and why TLS verification must stay on.
